--- title: "From rows to effects" description: "Annotate an experiment, declare its metrics, fit the universal model, and read its effects." order: 1 jupyter: python3 --- This article analyzes the running example of the [conditionally sufficient statistics post](https://jeffwong.github.io/posts/conditionally_sufficient_statistics/): a streaming service prompts accounts to turn on a playback setting, ramps the prompt from 5% to 50% of new accounts over four days, and measures each profile's hours watched and rebuffers per play. It is a clustered encouragement design with adaptive assignment and a ratio metric, which is every feature of the universal model at once. The data is simulated, so we also know the truth. ::: {#dda9b138 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl import ume from ume.testing import simulate_accounts, truth df = simulate_accounts(20_000, seed=2026) df.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## 1. Annotate We name the role of each column. The cluster is the unit of randomization and of independence; the instrument is the randomized prompt; the treatment is whether the profile turned the setting on; the cohort is the day, within which the prompt had one propensity. Each covariate gets a fixed reference point $x_{ref}$. ::: {#2407e249 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} exp = ume.annotate( df, cluster="account", instrument="Z", treatment="T", cohort="day", covariates=ume.covariates(x1=2.0, x2=2.0, kids=0, device=ume.categorical(reference="tv")), ) exp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

Frame operations pass through, and results that keep the annotated columns stay annotated: ::: {#d42750c4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} type(exp.filter(pl.col("day") > 1)).__name__, type(exp.group_by("day").agg(pl.col("y").mean())).__name__ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ('Experiment', 'DataFrame') ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Metrics Hours is a mean metric. Rebuffers per play is a ratio. The library derives the outcome columns, including the $T \cdot Y$ columns that identify the compliers' own levels: ::: {#1cb87a9b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} exp = exp.metrics(ume.mean("y", name="hours"), ume.ratio("N", "D", name="rebuffers_per_play")) exp.outcome_columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
